questions.q: What does a blocking_session_id value of 0 mean for a row in sys.dm_exec_requests?
options: That request is not currently blocked
The session has been killed
The request is the head of a blocking chain
The request is running with sysadmin permissions
questions.explain: blocking_session_id is 0 when a request isn't waiting on any other session, and non-zero when it is — set to the blocking session's ID.

questions.q: How does Section 2's query identify the head of a blocking chain?
options: It finds a blocking_session_id value that never itself appears as a session_id with blocking_session_id <> 0 — meaning it blocks others without being blocked
It finds the session with the highest cpu_time
It finds the session that has been connected the longest
It finds the session with the lowest session_id number
questions.explain: The head of the chain blocks other sessions but is not itself waiting on anyone — found by excluding any blocking_session_id that also shows up as a blocked session_id.

questions.q: Why does killing the session at the end of a five-session blocking chain typically fail to resolve the incident?
options: Because every session in the chain is ultimately waiting on the head of the chain, not on each other directly
Because KILL only works on the session with the lowest session_id
Because ending a session at the end of a chain always causes a deadlock
It actually does resolve the incident every time
questions.explain: Each blocked session in the chain is waiting on the head, whether directly or transitively. Removing a session at the end leaves the head still holding its lock, so everyone else remains blocked.

questions.q: In Section 3's expensive-query ranking, what does a row with a non-zero blocking_session_id combined with high cpu_time usually indicate?
options: A query that is both resource-expensive and currently blocked — often the single most important row in the output
A query that has already finished executing
A query running under the sa login
A query that cannot be a valid result, since blocked queries never consume CPU
questions.explain: blocking_session_id is carried into the expensive-query section too, so a row that's both expensive and blocked stands out as needing attention on two fronts at once.

questions.q: Why do the blocking-chain queries and the expensive-query ranking belong in the same incident-response script rather than two separate ones?
options: Because 'the database is slow' can mean either something is blocked or something is simply expensive, and a DBA needs both answers in the same incident
Because sys.dm_exec_requests cannot be queried more than once per session
Because SQL Server requires blocking and CPU checks to run in the same batch
There's no real benefit — they could just as easily be separate scripts
questions.explain: Blocking and raw resource cost are two distinct, common causes of a database feeling slow. Combining both checks into one script means a single run covers both possibilities instead of guessing which one applies first.
